mcqs.question: A graph has 3 disconnected pieces. What's the total traversal work across all pieces to count them, compared to a single traversal on a fully-connected graph of the same total size?
options: Three times as much work, since three separate traversals are launched
The same total O(V+E), since each node and edge is still touched exactly once overall, just split across multiple traversal calls
Less work, since each traversal only covers part of the graph
It depends on which node the first traversal starts from
mcqs.explanation: Each node and edge is visited exactly once across the entire process regardless of how many separate components it's split into — launching a fresh traversal per unvisited node doesn't repeat work, since previously-visited nodes are always skipped. The total remains O(V+E), the same as a single traversal over an equally-sized connected graph.

mcqs.question: In the BFS-based bipartiteness check, why does the outer loop iterate over every node in range(n) rather than just running BFS once from node 0?
options: Running BFS only from node 0 would be too slow for large graphs
The graph might be disconnected, and a component not reachable from node 0 would never get checked, silently reporting as bipartite even if it isn't
It's required to correctly assign colors 0 and 1 alternately
It has no effect — a single BFS from node 0 always suffices
mcqs.explanation: If the graph has multiple disconnected pieces, a traversal starting only at node 0 never reaches the other pieces, so any non-bipartite structure hiding there would go completely unchecked and the function would incorrectly return true. Both approaches have the same time complexity when they check the same nodes, and color alternation is handled at the neighbor-assignment step, not by the outer loop itself.

mcqs.question: What is the precise relationship between bipartiteness and cycles in a graph?
options: A graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no cycles at all
A graph is bipartite if and only if all of its cycles are even-length; any odd-length cycle makes it non-bipartite
Bipartiteness has no relationship to cycle length
A graph is bipartite if and only if it contains at least one even-length cycle
mcqs.explanation: Walking around any cycle forces colors to alternate, and an odd number of edges in the cycle forces a contradiction — the last node ends up needing to match the color of its neighbor. Graphs with no cycles at all (trees) are always bipartite, and having some even cycle doesn't guarantee bipartiteness if another odd cycle also exists — the condition is about ALL cycles being even, not just having no cycles or having one even cycle.

mcqs.question: A directed graph has one node from which every other node is reachable. Is the graph strongly connected?
options: Not necessarily — strongly connected requires every node to reach every other node, and this only establishes reachability from one specific node
Yes, that condition is the exact definition of strongly connected
Yes, as long as the graph also has no cycles
This scenario is impossible in a directed graph
mcqs.explanation: Strong connectivity requires mutual reachability between every pair of nodes, following edge directions both ways — one node reaching everything else says nothing about whether other nodes can reach back to it or to each other, as in a star graph with all edges pointing outward from the center. This scenario is entirely possible and common, and cycles (or their absence) don't determine strong connectivity on their own.

mcqs.question: A bipartiteness-check implementation only runs BFS starting from node 0, then returns whether that traversal found any color conflict. On a fully-connected test graph, it passes every test. What's the hidden risk?
options: There is no risk — a fully-connected passing test proves the implementation is correct for all graphs
The bug only appears on disconnected graphs, where components unreachable from node 0 are never checked and could be non-bipartite without detection
The risk is that BFS is the wrong traversal to use for this check at all
The implementation will crash on any graph with more than one component
mcqs.explanation: Testing exclusively on connected graphs can't expose a missing outer loop, because there's only one component to check in the first place — the bug specifically requires a disconnected input to surface, which is exactly why it's easy to miss until production data includes one. BFS is a perfectly valid traversal for this check, and the missing outer loop causes silently wrong answers, not a crash.

mcqs.question: A directed star graph has all edges pointing outward from a single center node to every leaf. Which of these is true?
options: The graph is strongly connected, since the center can reach every leaf
The graph has no meaningful connectivity property at all
The graph is weakly connected (or reachable from the center), but not strongly connected, since leaves cannot reach the center or each other
The graph is bipartite by definition because it's a star shape
mcqs.explanation: The center reaching every leaf only establishes reachability from one node — leaves have no outgoing edges back to the center or to each other, so mutual reachability (required for strong connectivity) fails completely. It does have a meaningful connectivity property (weak connectivity, or single-source reachability), just not the strong one; bipartiteness is an entirely separate property unrelated to a graph's star shape.
